children: The recent correction in global AI-related stocks could present a buying opportunity as the artificial intelligence infrastructure cycle is far from over, according to Bhavtosh Vajpayee, International Head of Technology Research at CLSA.
Speaking at the CITIC CLSA India Forum, Vajpayee said the AI build-out is expected to continue through the rest of the decade despite investor concerns over funding, returns and policy changes.

CLSA expects AI infrastructure spending to remain elevated for several years as hyperscalers continue investing to protect their market position. Vajpayee also said Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) remains the firm's preferred way to play the AI theme, with its 2027 capital expenditure guidance likely to shape expectations for the broader AI ecosystem.

"The build is robust and will continue through the rest of the decade," Vajpayee said, adding that recent weakness reflects "a degree of tiredness, exhaustion among investors" rather than a structural change in the AI story.
He said concerns surrounding Nvidia, delays in the Anthropic IPO and questions around AI returns have weighed on sentiment, but such corrections are common during major technology investment cycles.
AI spending likely to stay elevated
Vajpayee said investors expecting hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Google and Meta to quickly return to strong free cash flow generation may have to wait longer.
"It is a reality of the new AI build that more money has to be spent," he said, explaining that companies are prioritising AI infrastructure investments to maintain their competitive position.
According to him, capital expenditure intensity has structurally increased and is unlikely to moderate for several years because hyperscalers do not want to lose leadership in AI.
Over time, however, he expects AI monetisation to improve as enterprise adoption expands.
"As you head into the 2030s... you will have a much bigger economy dependent on AI... and hopefully more free cash flows," Vajpayee said.
Political changes unlikely to derail AI expansion

Responding to concerns that changes in the US political landscape could slow AI investments, Vajpayee said the AI infrastructure boom began under the previous administration and is unlikely to reverse.
He acknowledged that future governments may introduce additional regulatory guardrails, particularly around energy usage and natural gas, but said fears of restrictions on data centers are overdone.
"To think that data centers will be banned... is quite an extreme opinion. We don't agree with that," he said.
Chip supply remains the biggest constraint
Contrary to concerns that data center construction delays could slow AI adoption, CLSA believes semiconductor availability remains the real bottleneck.

Vajpayee said the firm's research estimates nearly 200 gigawatts of data centres are currently under construction globally outside China, while expected chip production from TSMC would only support around 110-120 gigawatts.
"Essentially, there are too few chips to power the data centers which are under construction," he said.
Because of that imbalance, he believes delays at individual data center projects are unlikely to disrupt the broader AI investment cycle.
TSMC remains CLSA's preferred AI investment
Asked for his top investment idea within the AI ecosystem, Vajpayee named Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC).
He said semiconductor production ultimately determines the pace of AI deployment, making TSMC's capital expenditure plans for 2027 a key indicator for investors.
"It is Taiwan Semiconductor," Vajpayee said. "It is futile to make a projection of anything downstream without figuring out how many chips TSMC can provide."
Anthropic remains central to AI monetisation
Vajpayee also said investor attention on Anthropic is justified because the company has become one of the clearest indicators of AI commercialisation.
According to CLSA, Anthropic accounts for roughly 11% of global AI token usage outside China, while representing an even larger share of investor attention.

"Nearly a third of all the dollars... attributed to AI come through the Anthropic top line," he said, adding that investor focus on the company's IPO is understandable, although he declined to comment on the offering itself.

title: CLSA says AI infrastructure spending will stay high, chip shortage to remain key constraint
